access: Author/coordinator only until independent reviewer solutions are frozen.
method: Independently translated exact image-checked Old English before seeing any other private translation or draft key. Cook original notes and the larger source context were consulted as evidence.

readings.translation: It is also rich in veins of metals—copper and iron, lead and silver. Here jet is also found; the stone is a black gem. If one puts it in a fire, then snakes flee away there.
notes: Initial it refers to Britain/the island from the preceding context, supplied separately in English.
Hine is masculine accusative singular, referring to se stān, the stone.
The source attributes the flight of snakes to jet put on a fire; do not recast this as a modern scientific finding.
The Latin and Cook note1 establish berende on as rich in / productive of here; do not translate simply carrying on ores.
Næddran has two d in the source running text. Flēoð is from flēon flee, not flēogan fly.

readings.translation:
Then, after a long time, we lifted our gaze and looked far off. We saw on Farne, the island, the father Æthelwald, dear to God, coming out of his retreat, to observe our voyage and see what might happen to us, because he had heard the crash of the storms and of the surging sea.

When he too looked at us and saw us in distress and despair, he bent his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and prayed for our safety and our lives. And when he completed the prayer, he at once both calmed the swollen sea and stilled the storm, so that the whole fury of the storm ceased, and favorable winds brought us to land through a very calm sea. When we came up onto land and also carried our ship up from the waves, immediately the same storm returned and came on, which had ceased for our sake for a little while; it was very great and strong all that day. Thus people could clearly understand that the brief period of calm which had occurred there had been granted from heaven at the prayers of the man of God for the sake of our rescue.
notes: The first ðā wæs æfter langum fæce ðæt introduces the lapse of time before the observers lift their gaze; no full prior storm passage is inserted into the source text.
Wolde plus scēawian/gesēon is supported within the purpose clause; may watch and see or in order to watch and see is preferable to making private desire the only meaning.
Cook note142.17 calls ūtgangende a present participle used for Latin past participle; came out / having come out is defensible under the note.
Gelumpe is third-person singular preterite subjunctive of gelimpan, what might happen/befall us; source-only local help.
Geseah governs an understood us and gesętte bēon. Translation saw us distressed does not imply gesętte is a new productive finite verb.
Cook143.1 and142.7 contextualize wæs gebiddende as a simple past. Wæs blinnende likewise belongs to the supplied local periphrasis; no universal progressive equation.
Source sǣ is masculine in these determiner and genitive combinations, matching the actual Unit1 productive masculine forms; the separately supplied feminine genitive is not the analysis here.
The literal singular ūre hǣle/ūrum līfe refers to the party’s safety/life. Lives is natural English, not an Old English plural claim.
The source superlative smyltestan may be rendered very calm or calmest under the supplied help, without teaching a general elative system.
Gestilde in the relative clause is contextually anterior; English had ceased makes the sequence explicit without claiming a distinct Old English pluperfect.
Final forgiefen means given/granted, not forgiven; Cook143.18 explicitly directs that meaning. Note143.16 is Lat. evasionis, supporting escape/rescue.
The wind returns after the people and ship are ashore. The narrator sees the limited calm as a grant for this rescue, not a permanent ending of storms.
